articles.title: The AI boom has handed the Fed an inflation problem that rate hikes may not fix
articles.text:
The AI boom created an inflation problem. What's the Fed to do?
Marketplace®
Every story is an economic story
Donate
Nov 13, 2026
The AI boom has handed the Fed an inflation problem that rate hikes may not fix
Fed Chair Warsh will convene a forum on Monday to look at AI’s impact on the economy and monetary policy.
The Federal Reserveby Kristin Schwab
Download
AI is fueling inflation, yes, but it's also fueling economic growth. Could monetary policy aimed at cooling that inflation also hamper positive economic growth?
Spencer Platt/Getty Images
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh will be in San Francisco on Monday, Nov. 15, to talk about how artificial intelligence might affect the economy and, in turn, monetary policy. The event has been planned for a while — before the Nvidia fallout and the midterm election outcomes.
Still, AI isn’t going anywhere. The central bank continues to weigh just how much AI demand is responsible for current inflation.
Short term, there isn’t a lot of debate here: Investment in AI is boosting the price of chips, which in turn raises the prices of electronics including phones, computers and gaming consoles.
But that’s not all, said former Fed economist Ken Kuttner.
“We know that the AI buildout is putting pressure on the demand for labor, the demand for goods and services and in some places it’s actually raising energy prices,” he said.
Kuttner said the better question is whether inflation from AI demand is a short-term thing. The problem is, there’s not a lot of time to figure that out.
“It would be a much easier call now if it weren’t for the fact that we’re already well above the desired rate of inflation,” he said.
Plus, the central bank is dealing with a bunch of other problems that push up prices, like the war in Iran.
AI and inflation
June 2026: Many economists believe that AI will lead to more inflation. Why?
June 2026: Could AI eventually make things cheaper?
April 2026: There's no such thing as free AI
January 2026: Why the cost of a new laptop might go up this year
Another layer here? AI buildout is fueling the economy. Companies have big appetites to borrow and spend. And the AI-powered corner of the stock market means some consumers have big appetites to borrow and spend, too.
“It’s making many people very wealthy. And so they may be more likely to buy houses and consume,” said former Fed governor Randy Kroszner.
To slow consumption, the Fed is likely to raise rates in December. But Kroszner said it’s probably not going to curb AI spending.
“There’s so much excitement about AI that, you know, half a percentage point higher interest rates, not sure that’s really going to slow down AI investment,” he said.
This Nvidia scandal, the AI data center backlash, and the question of whether the sector is moving too fast, could put a speed bump in investment.
Still, EY-Parthenon Chief Economy Gregory Daco thinks AI will keep adding to the inflation soup.
“That’s likely to linger over the next 12 to 24 months,” he said, and help build a case for more interest rate hikes next year.

articles.title: What will happen at Nvidia's impending earnings call?
articles.text:
Nvidia's upcoming earnings call could spell trouble
Marketplace®
Every story is an economic story
Donate
Nov 13, 2026
What will happen at Nvidia's impending earnings call?
Nvidia has had a scandal-filled week. It has an earnings call on Tuesday.
Companiesby Stephanie Hughes
Download
Nvidia's quarterly earnings call comes at a tumultuous time for the AI company.
Sean Gallup/Getty Images
Nvidia has a quarterly earnings call on Tuesday.
Awkward timing, to say the least.
It’s one of the biggest public events of the year for the corporate communications team under normal circumstances. But, of course, circumstances are far from normal: The CEO of 33 years — the only one the company has ever had — has stepped down amid a scandal or three. The chief financial officer is the new caretaker in the top job.
Analysts, investors, and the public at large want to hear everything that leadership has to say, because the value of Nvidia stock and how well the company does are critical to the AI boom — and therefore to the economy at large.
Earnings calls are pretty much always scripted, but Karen Woody, a professor at the Washington and Lee University of Law said that this one in particular will be especially planned-out.
“The first thing you do is you do run every single word by the attorneys,” she said.
Lawyers are always involved when companies disclose their financial results. However, now that government investigations may be on the way, Woody said that Nvidia will want to be extra careful about its words.
She said the company will also want get across a sense of continuity.
“They need to operate as if this is clearly something this company can get through, and … you know, the trains still are on time,” Woody said.
Woody said one benefit of having the chief financial officer step up is that she knows Nvidia’s business. Still, she and her comms team will be working through the weekend.
“I’m sure there are a number of rehearsals that have been going on,” said Anne-Taylor Adams, vice president of marketing and communications at Antenna, and has worked in corporate communications for a few publicly traded companies.
Roughly half of an earnings call is prepared remarks. The rest is Q&A from stock analysts, which means that the Nvidia execs will have to field some questions about what went down.
“You try and contain things with the facts that you know and can actually stand behind, and then really get back to the business of the quarter,” Adams said.
Adams said that it’s important for the communications team to know everything that might come out.
“And this is probably particularly gnarly,” she said, “because it is dealing with personal, familial relationships.”
Going forward with the earnings call despite the crisis is a signal of business as usual, said Woody.
“You know, basically,” she said, “‘Nothing to see here.'“

articles.title: Why is there no "lemon law" for homes?
articles.text:
Why is there no "lemon law" for homes?
Marketplace®
Every story is an economic story
Donate
Nov 13, 2026
Why is there no "lemon law" for homes?
Even if there's no direct lemon law like there is for automobiles, there are still various protections that exist for homebuyers who find unpleasant surprises.
I've Always Wondered ...by Janet Nguyen
kudou/Getty Images Plus
This is just one of the stories from our “I’ve Always Wondered” series, where we tackle all of your questions about the world of business, no matter how big or small. Ever wondered if recycling is worth it? Or how store brands stack up against name brands? Check out more from the series here.
Brent Gray from Richardson, Texas, asks:
Why is there no lemon law for homes? We purchased a flipped home in 2021 and found many issues.
Daniel Whitney Sr. — the managing partner of Whitney, LLP in Maryland — has represented homebuyers with issues running the gamut, including structurally unsound foundations, leaky roofs and hidden mold in the walls.
"Just horror stories," Whitney said.
One couple he's representing purchased a new home advertised as being built in 2025. Turns out it was actually a rehabilitated farmhouse from 1912.
"Shortly after they moved in, they had to move out because the plumbing was not up to code, and the sewage smell throughout the whole house was so overwhelming that it was a health hazard," Whitney said.
If you buy a defective vehicle, customers are entitled to a repair, refund or replacement vehicle under lemon laws, which will vary by state. While there is no "lemon law" for homebuyers, various protections do still exist if a seller lied to you about any defects or purposefully omitted key information about your home, and you can take legal action against them.
Many states require disclosure statements, mandating sellers to list any defects or details like how old the roof is, whether the heating and air conditioning system works and whether there are any electrical problems, said Julie Patterson Forrester Rogers, a law professor at Southern Methodist University in Texas.
But that doesn't stop some sellers, like the ones Whitney has won against in court. If the housing market is especially competitive, some buyers have actually foregone inspections or inspection contingencies, which would normally allow them to back out on offers contingent upon any findings.
When it comes to the purchase of a new home from a builder, almost every state recognizes implied warranties, which protect homebuyers when it comes to defects in their house, Rogers said.
One defect might be having a home with a roof that is always going to leak, Rogers said.
"Because a builder is unlikely to agree to undoing the sale or paying damages, a lawsuit would usually be necessary. However, states often require by statute that the builder be given an opportunity to fix the problem first," Rogers said.
Implied warranties will vary state by state. In Texas, there are two warranties, one focused on habitability (you could sue, for example, if a defective sewer line makes your house uninhabitable) and one on workmanship, which is based on quality work, Rogers said.
"The real difference between liability for an ordinary seller versus a builder seller is that the builder makes the warranty, and that means even if they don't know there's a problem, you can go back against that builder on the warranty. Whereas if just an ordinary seller doesn't know about a problem, then they aren't going to have liability," Rogers said.
But there are still various protections for homebuyers who are buying from ordinary sellers.
If someone sells a house to you and claims it has a brand new roof when it's actually 20-years-old and leaks, that could be considered fraudulent misrepresentation and you would have a cause of action against the seller, Rogers said.
If there's termite damage to the house and instead of fixing the problem the seller puts up new drywall to cover it up, that could be considered fraudulent concealment, and you would also have a cause of action, Rogers said.
You can also be protected against negligent misrepresentation, in which a seller makes false statements without having exercised reasonable care.
There are various ways of assessing damages. Whitney said typically, the legal remedy is to sue for the cost to repair the house so that it aligns with how the home was represented. Sometimes, there might be a buyback.
In one case, there was a house flipper who sold his client a house with major structural flaws.
"We came up with an agreement where the flipper would buy it back for the sales price and pay all closing costs and attorney's fees, and hold my client harmless from any future claims that a subsequent buyer might have," he said.
In another case, back in September, Whitney said he had a seven-day trial against a listing agent who sold a property with unpermitted work and structural hazards. The jury awarded the plaintiffs $234,000 in damages.
You can even get compensation if the square footage in your house was calculated incorrectly by an appraiser, Whitney said.
As for what makes a case likely to win? Whitney said you need to have a clearly defined problem and clear evidence that either the seller or the agent knew about it or should have known about it.
Sometimes that means doing some digging around.
"For instance, I had a termite case in Baltimore City," Whitney said. "Seller denied having any knowledge of termites, and I found out that it was a rental property before it was sold to my client. Well, talking to the neighbors, turns out this was not a very nice person, and so they were very happy to talk to me about this, and I was able to get the names of the prior renters."
Whitney said it's "unconscionable" when buyers purchase their dream home, only to encounter an unsafe house with issues like termite damage or a failed septic system.

articles.title: Checking in on the Oklahoma economy
articles.text:
How SNAP cuts and challenges for farmers are playing out in Oklahoma
Marketplace®
Every story is an economic story
Donate
Nov 12, 2026
Checking in on the Oklahoma economy
Anna Pope, multimedia journalist at KOSU and Harvest Public Media, discusses some of the big economic news stories coming out of Oklahoma.
Economic Pulseby Kimberly Adams and Emma Condon
Download
Al Drago/Getty Images
As part of our Economic Pulse series, “Marketplace Morning Report” checks in with journalists from local public media outlets across the country to hear about the economic stories they’re following in their communities and states.
This week, “Marketplace Morning Report” host Kimberly Adams spoke with Anna Pope, a multimedia journalist covering agriculture and rural affairs for Oklahoma’s KOSU and Harvest Public Media.
She came on the program to discuss how SNAP enrollment decline is showing up in the Oklahoma economy and how a drought has impacted the state’s agriculture industry. The following is an edited transcript of Kimberly and Anna’s conversation.
Kimberly Adams: So, let's talk SNAP enrollment, which has been falling around the country, but it's hitting Oklahoma particularly hard. What are some of the numbers you're seeing?
Anna Pope: Yeah. So, since July 2025 to July 2026, we've seen about a 22.5% decrease in SNAP shoppers in the state, and so that's roughly about 154,000 Oklahomans falling off the program.
Adams: And why are they falling off the program?
Pope: Well, there's a number of things that have happened in the SNAP program since the Trump administration took office again; a lot of changes on a state and federal level. You know, we've seen through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, namely that Congress has expanded work requirements for participants, scrapped the SNAP education program, cut off eligibility for certain legal immigrants, and shifted hundreds of millions of dollars in administrative and benefit costs to states. So, all of these things are kind of happening all at once.
Adams: Do you have any sense yet of the impact that those changes, especially people falling off of SNAP, is having for the Oklahoma economy?
Pope: Yeah. So, because of how many people have fallen off the program and SNAP, a lot of people who haven't had problems recertifying before are having problems, and so when you have less participants in the program, that means there's less dollars being spent on a local level, right? So, I went to a rural area in north Oklahoma — Pond Creek, and I spoke to a local grocer there, and they've seen about a 90% drop in SNAP sales. And that doesn't just impact their grocery store. That's also a local economy because what we know about SNAP is that it's a multiplier, right? Figures show about every dollar spent in a local economy; it's probably about $1.50 returning to that local economy.
Understanding changes to SNAP
From August 2026: More than six decades after it was signed into law, the program known as SNAP is at risk
From July 2026: A year since Trump's big tax bill, SNAP enrollment has fallen dramatically
From February 2026: More states ban SNAP recipients from buying certain foods
From January 2026: States are tightening limits on what SNAP recipients can do with their benefits
From October 2025: The loss of SNAP benefits could have ripple effects across the economy
Adams: You also visited several food banks that are helping to feed people who've lost their benefits. What did you see there?
Pope: One of the places I visited to learn more about what food insecurity has looked like in Oklahoma communities as these changes have unfolded was at the Lawton Food Bank, and there I met Alex Minter McCann. She's the executive director of the Lawton Food Bank, and she has seen more demand for these services.
Alex Minter McCann: The biggest thing that we are trying to project and prepare for is just how many of our clients that receive SNAP funds currently are going to be coming to the food bank needing additional food than what they're currently getting right now.
Pope: So, they're trying to predict how many people will need this service as they fall off this program, but then also how many people will just be seeking the service merely because they're facing more costs at the grocery store.
Adams: I want to switch gears to a bit of a different topic. Oklahoma experienced a drought this summer and early fall. How has that impacted the agricultural sector, particularly cattle production?
Pope: Sure. So, when there's less rain overall, there's less moisture in the ground, and then there's less grass for cattle, right? And so, producers had to roll out hay and spend money on that hay earlier than expected. And then also, there's less water in ponds, or ponds have gone dry, and so that means producers are having to haul water out to fields. And that's very work-intensive, and it's an expense as well for producers. And so, a lot of people have been, you know, maybe looking at the situation and just anecdotally, whenever I've talked to producers, some of them have been selling their cows as they've gone through this process.
Adams: Did the federal or state government step in at all to help folks through the drought?
Pope: Yes, we do have some emergency drought funds here in the state, and people can apply for them. But what we know from droughts in general is, while every bit of assistance is helpful, droughts also, depending on the situation, can cost billions of dollars in the agriculture industry. And we don't have those figures just yet. The lasting impacts kind of remain to be seen, because it just takes a while to work through the system to work through everything.
Adams: Back in August, President Trump announced a deal that was supposed to temporarily allow more beef to enter the U.S. as a way to lower beef prices in particular. How did the cattlemen in Oklahoma react to that news?
Pope: They didn't like it, and so a lot of people in the state really view beef as the one bright spo

articles.title: From tariffs to data centers, Michigan's big economic stories
articles.text:
Ahead of Michigan's midterms, tariffs and data centers are key issues
Marketplace®
Every story is an economic story
Donate
Oct 23, 2026
From tariffs to data centers, Michigan's big economic stories
Robyn Vincent, a producer and host at WDET in Detroit, discusses some of the big economic news stories out of her state.
Economic Pulseby Kimberly Adams and Emma Condon
Download
The Gordie Howe International Bridge connects Windsor, Ontario, and Detroit, Michigan. It opened up in July, despite continued trade tension between the U.S. and Canada.
Jeff Kowalsky/AFP via Getty Images
As part of our Economic Pulse series, “Marketplace Morning Report” checks in with journalists from local public media outlets across the country to hear about the economic stories they’re following in their communities and states.
This week, “Marketplace Morning Report” host Kimberly Adams spoke with Robyn Vincent. She’s the host and producer on WDET’s “The Metro” in Detroit.
She came on the program to discuss how the trade war with Canada is impacting the Michigan economy — plus some fights over data centers and high utility bills in the state. The following is an edited transcript of Kimberly and Robyn’s conversation.
Kimberly Adams: So, tariffs are a huge story where you are in Detroit. The Trump administration has imposed 50% tariffs on certain Canadian goods. You have so much commerce back and forth across the border there in Michigan. How have these tariffs affected the Michigan economy?
Robyn Vincent: Yeah, Kimberly, Michigan is hit harder than most states, and the short answer to why that is is that we're on both ends of this. So, Michigan buys more auto parts from Canada than any other state and ships them more than any other state. So, we get taxed coming and going. I spoke with Jason Miller, who studies supply chains at Michigan State University, and he told me so far, it's showing up in jobs more than in prices. He said importers have absorbed most of the tariffs rather than raise prices, but Michigan has lost about 4,000 jobs when it comes to people who are making auto parts in the last year, and that's according to the state's automotive dashboard.
Adams: The automotive industry is not the only one feeling the pinch. There's also the tourism industry. How has that been affected?
Vincent: Yeah, I mean something you have to remember, Kimberly, is Detroit is a border town. Windsor, Ontario, sits directly across the river from downtown Detroit.
In July, a new bridge opened between Detroit and Windsor. It's the longest bridge of its kind in North America. Canada paid for nearly all of it, close to $5 billion. Now, here's what's very telling about that: the two countries were supposed to cut the ribbon together. Canada called that off. They held their own ceremony on their side of the river and pointed to the president's tariff threats.
A lot of Canadians are likely to not use this new bridge. Visit Detroit, the regional tourism bureau, tells me that visitation from Canada has been running about 30% below normal since 2025. But I've talked to local business owners who feel that number is much lower. That there are many more Canadians who are choosing not to cross over, not to spend their money in Detroit.
I went to Eastern Market — that's Detroit's public market. It's the place you go on a Saturday morning for fresh produce and artisanal cheeses and locally made goods like jewelry and leather handbags. Vendors there tell me their Canadian regulars have pretty much stopped coming.

Adams: We're coming up on the midterm elections. How much are the issues of trade and tariffs and its impact on Michigan coming up with these candidates as we get down to the final days before voting?
Vincent: Yeah, they're talking about it a lot. Democrat Abdul El-Sayed calls the president's approach “chaotic,” “ham-fisted,” “self-serving.” He's got the United Auto Workers behind him. Republican Mike Rogers says he's ready to work with the president on the tariffs, the ones that are working at least, and he says that he's ready to push back on the ones that aren't.
They are both making their pleas to voters right now that they can make change, that they will be agents of change in this moment when so many voters are angry and want to see the tariffs and the trade war come to an end.
Adams: I want to shift gears now. Data centers have become a flashpoint across the country. How is that debate playing out in Michigan?
Vincent: Yeah, it's playing out in a few different places right now. Van Buren Township, which sits about 25 miles west of Detroit, is an area with farmland, subdivisions, and industrial parks, and so Big Tech has been eyeing it. And last week, it approved a Google data center that will draw a gigawatt of electricity. That's about what 750,000 homes use.
The township and Wayne County are forgiving an estimated $125 million in local taxes over the next 12 years. Residents packed meetings for 10 months, asking the board to reject it. The township supervisor, Kevin McNamara, told my colleague Quinn Kleinfelter that he didn't have the option to say no.
Kevin McNamara: A lot of them just don't seem to understand that data centers are legal. They say, “just say no.” You can't just say no. If you say no, you go to court, and the court decides what to do, and they decide how to build it. Matt Cardy/Getty Images
It's time once again for us to take the Marketplace Economic Pulse. That’s our series where we check in with reporters from local public media outlets across the country to tell us about the economic stories they’re following in their communities and states.
This week, “Marketplace Morning Report” host Kimberly Adams spoke with Jessica Meszaros. She’s a climate and environment reporter at Florida’s WUSF. She and her team have been working on their own series called The Cost of Power, which explores why energy bills are so high in the Sunshine State. The following is an edited transcript of Kimberly and Jessica’s conversation.
Kimberly Adams: Jessica, you found in your reporting that energy bills in Florida have jumped by as much as 70% over the past 10 years. What explains that?
Jessica Meszaros: Yeah, bills are so high, mostly because of consecutive rate hikes. You know, it’s every three years or so, companies are allowed to ask for a rate hike, and sometimes they would, sometimes they wouldn't in the past. But it's been consecutive; every time, we know that they will. There's also something called pass-through costs and other surcharges, which have pushed up prices faster than household incomes. And then Florida — in particular, Florida utilities — they're allowed to make the most return on equity than anywhere else, according to my sources. Like Florida Power & Light — it's the highest in the country of any major utility.
Above, the logo of Florida Power & Light at its solar farm in December 2023.
Marco Bello/AFP via Getty Images
Adams: Well, say more about the role of utility companies in all of this. That feels like quite the outlier.
Meszaros: Well, Florida has four major investor-owned utilities, and at the same time that these bills have been climbing, these investor-owned utilities made more than $6 billion in profits last year. Consumer advocates are pretty upset about that, and they think that profits should be capped, and that that's contributing as well to these bills rising.
Adams: What are some alternatives to this for-profit model?
Meszaros: Well, utilities can be run by a municipal government. We've seen that happen in Florida before. The last time was, I think, over a decade ago. But it can be costly. There are lawsuits. We know that two in particular in this region, in Saint Petersburg and in Clearwater, the cities were looking to remove themselves from Duke Energy Florida and run their own utility to bring down costs. But Clearwater decided to back off from that because the cost would be too much, in terms of that kind of transition and the lawsuits. But Saint Petersburg is still researching that, so that can be an alternative if the city is so willing. And we've heard from people in the community meetings during public hearings, saying that they want this.
Adams: Beyond the utility companies, there's also this government-appointed commission that is in charge of approving rate hikes. What have they been doing this whole time?
Meszaros: Yeah, so it's called the Florida Public Service Commission. It's five commissioners appointed by Florida's governor, and they've been accused of rubber-stamping a lot of these rate hikes and surcharges that have been tacked on. And there's been some call — like bipartisan support, really. Last year, we had two pieces of legislation — one from a Republican and one from a Democrat — trying to revamp this commission to get those caps on profits, as well as getting some people on the commission who specialize in utilities and specialize in the environment.
More from WUSF's energy reporting
What’s behind the high electricity bills crushing Floridians?
Fossil fuels vs. solar: Which should power Florida to lower energy bills?
How the Florida Public Service Commission affects what you pay for electricity
Adams: When the utilities are putting in for these rate hikes, what are they saying justifies it?
Meszaros: So, one of the big things is that Florida has the second-highest electricity consumption in the country, and the population keeps growing, so that leads utilities to continuously expand their rate base. And then also they're allowed to pass on capital expenditures onto customers, like when you build a power plant, for example. So, they're really incentivized to expand, but they're saying like, in order to expand, we need more money, basically.
Adams: This is affecting people all over Florida, but you and your colleagues focused on one man, Thaddeus Williams. Why did you feel it was important to highlight his story?
Meszaros: We felt it was important to highlight Thaddeus' story because, one, he's a renter, and electric bills don't just impact homeowners; it impacts everybody — people who rent, anyone who lives in Florida and pays an electric bill. And so, he's a 75-year-old retired veteran. He's living off Social Security, and he's also a single dad to an eight-year-old daughter. He pays about $200 to $300 a month for power, and it's his second-highest bill next to rent. Let's hear Thaddeus explain what he hears from his community members.
Thaddeus Williams: Everybody I talk to talks about, “Oh man, my electric bill is higher than it was last month,” and I know people who just wouldn't even pay the bill. They just said, “Well, I'm not gonna pay them.” And they live in the house with candles.
Adams: Candles, wow.
Meszaros: Yeah, it's important to note that Thaddeus himself turns off the lights and lives by candlelight to try to save on his energy bill. And he basically says sometimes his efforts don't work, and his bill has actually been higher sometimes after using less elect

Do you ever feel like you’re always on the brink of financial catastrophe, no matter how much money you have in your bank accounts? The term “money dysmorphia” describes the disconnect between our financial reality and how we actually feel about our finances, and nearly half of Gen Z and millennials struggle with it.
This week, Reema talks with writer Lindsey Stanberry and financial therapist Amanda Clayman about how childhood experiences and social comparison shape our perceptions of money, and what it takes to feel safe in an uncertain world.
A few takeaways from this episode:
Money dysmorphia can shape our spending habits, relationships, and even day-to-day decisions. “A lot of guilt. A lot of denial of things that you need,” Stanberry said. “Buying stuff that's inexpensive and then having to replace it because you didn’t shell out for the thing that's maybe a little bit more high quality.” Stanberry said one way to combat these patterns is to be intentional about what matters most to you. “You can feel good about your expenses if you’re being really thoughtful about how you’re spending your money.”
Be specific about what number would make you feel safe and work through the discomfort. “That gives a person feelings of like, ‘Yeah, I still have the feelings but I'm able to take the action that is consistent with my values and what's important to me,’” said Clayman, “and not necessarily just limited by these old echoes of fear that are attached to things like this.”
The goal is to build confidence in your ability to handle uncertainty rather than eliminate it. As Clayman put it, “The place that we can come to feel a greater sense of safety is not necessarily that the world is safe, but rather that I have the capacity to live and navigate through an unsafe world.”
Also in the episode, another edition of “Alice Gets Her Life Together.” This week, producer Alice Wilder debriefs with Reema on her largest purchase yet: a home.
